Choose the correct arrangement of the following exchanges to make a meaningful conversation.
a. Hoa: Oh, I'm sorry to hear that. Have you tried contacting the shop?
b. Nam: I ordered a pair of headphones online last week, but they arrived broken.
c. Nam: Yes, but they insist that the damage happened after delivery.
d. Hoa: In that case, you should check whether the courier took photos when dropping off the parcel.
e. Nam: Good idea. If they did, I'll have proof that it was already damaged.
questions.e: Nam kể sự việc (b) → Hoa an ủi, hỏi đã liên hệ cửa hàng chưa (a) → Nam trả lời 'Yes, but…' (c) → Hoa gợi ý 'In that case…' (d) → Nam đồng ý (e).

b. In addition, my experience as head of the school's environment club has taught me how to motivate others.
c. Over the past two years, I have organised several community clean-up campaigns involving more than a hundred participants.
d. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss my application with you in person.
e. I believe this combination of practical and leadership experience has prepared me well for the role.
Dear Ms Taylor,
questions.e: Mở thư nêu mục đích (a) → kinh nghiệm thứ nhất (c) → 'In addition' thêm kinh nghiệm lãnh đạo (b) → 'this combination of practical and leadership experience' tổng hợp cả c và b (e) → câu kết mong được phỏng vấn (d).

b. Birds rely on song to attract mates and defend their territory.
c. To be heard, some city birds appear to have adjusted by singing at a higher pitch or at quieter times of day.
d. Whether such changes come at a cost to the birds remains an open question.
e. In quiet forests, these songs can carry over long distances.
questions.e: Câu chủ đề (b) → 'these songs' trong rừng yên tĩnh (e) → 'however' tương phản: ở đô thị ồn ào (a) → chim thích nghi 'To be heard' (c) → 'such changes' – câu kết mở (d).

a. Researchers argue that the key lies not in motivation but in the design of one's environment.
b. Many people start the new year with ambitious plans to exercise more or read every day.
c. For example, someone who places a book on their pillow each morning is far more likely to read before sleeping.

questions.ctx:
[I] Walk through almost any park or university campus and you are likely to notice narrow strips of bare earth cutting across the grass. [II] These informal trails, known as desire paths, are created not by planners but by the repeated footsteps of people taking the route they actually prefer. [III] Very often, that route is simply the shortest distance between two points, even if it means ignoring a carefully designed pavement. [IV]
For many years, the typical response of landscape managers was to fight these paths. Fences were put up, signs asked visitors to keep off the grass, and bare patches were reseeded. Such measures, however, rarely succeeded for long. As soon as the barriers were removed or ignored, walkers returned to their preferred line, and the path reappeared.
Some designers have since come to see desire paths in a more positive light. Rather than treating them as acts of vandalism, they read them as honest feedback about how a space is really used. A few campuses have even delayed laying permanent walkways until the first months after opening, waiting to see where the grass wears thin before paving those routes.
The idea has spread beyond parks. In digital design, the term is sometimes used for the shortcuts users invent when software does not work the way they expect – for instance, emailing files to themselves because a sharing function is too complicated. Here, too, the lesson is the same: when people repeatedly go around a system, the problem may lie with the system rather than with the people.
Of course, not every desire path should be paved. Some cross fragile habitats or create safety risks. But noticing them is a useful reminder that good design begins with observing behaviour, not merely with predicting it.

questions.q: The word 'fragile' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.e: 'fragile habitats' = môi trường sống mong manh, dễ bị tổn hại → 'easily damaged'.

questions.ctx:
In many classrooms, the pen is steadily giving way to the keyboard. Students take notes on laptops, submit essays online and may go days without writing more than a signature by hand. To some, this shift is simply progress: typing is faster, easier to edit and produces text that anyone can read. Yet a number of researchers and teachers have begun to ask whether something valuable is being lost along the way.
One argument concerns note-taking. Because most people can type far more quickly than they can write, laptop users are able to record lectures almost word for word. This might seem like an advantage, but some studies suggest that it can encourage a kind of mechanical transcription in which information passes from ear to screen without being properly processed. Students writing by hand, unable to keep up with the speaker, are forced to select, summarise and rephrase – activities that may help them understand and remember the material.
A second argument focuses on early learning. Forming letters by hand requires children to coordinate fine movements and to pay close attention to shape, and some researchers believe this process helps young learners recognise letters more readily when reading. Pressing a key, by contrast, produces a perfect letter with a single, identical movement, regardless of which letter is chosen.
None of this means that schools should abandon technology. Typing is an indispensable skill, and digital tools offer benefits that paper cannot match, from instant access to information to support for students with certain disabilities. The evidence on handwriting is also still developing, and not every study has reached the same conclusions. What the debate does suggest is that the choice between pen and keyboard is not merely a matter of convenience. Different tools may encourage different ways of thinking, and educators would be wise to consider which kind of thinking a particular task demands.

a. Mai: That sounds ideal. Is there an entrance fee?
b. Tuan: There's a new art exhibition at the museum this weekend. Would you like to go?

Choose the correct arrangement of the sentences to make a meaningful letter.
a. Unfortunately, when the package arrived, two of the four items were missing.
b. I am writing to express my dissatisfaction with an order I placed on your website on 3 March.
c. I would therefore be grateful if you could send the missing items or issue a full refund within fourteen days.
d. When I contacted your customer service team, I was told that the problem would be resolved within 48 hours, but I have heard nothing since.
e. I have attached a copy of my receipt for your reference.
Dear Sir or Madam,
questions.e: Nêu mục đích thư (b) → sự cố thiếu hàng (a) → đã liên hệ nhưng không được giải quyết (d) → 'therefore' đề nghị gửi hàng/ hoàn tiền (c) → đính kèm hóa đơn (e).

a. This is because switching between languages requires the brain to constantly select one system while suppressing the other.
b. Speaking two languages is often seen mainly as a practical skill for travel or work.
c. Over time, this mental exercise may strengthen abilities such as attention control and multitasking.
d. However, a growing body of research suggests that bilingualism may also shape the way the brain functions.
e. Even so, scientists continue to debate how large and long-lasting these advantages really are.
questions.e: Quan niệm phổ biến (b) → 'However' quan điểm mới (d) → 'This is because' giải thích (a) → 'this mental exercise' (= việc chuyển đổi ngôn ngữ ở a) (c) → 'Even so… these advantages' (e).

a. What mattered instead was a shared sense among members that they could speak up without fear of embarrassment.
b. When analysing the data, the researchers expected the best-performing groups to be those with the most talented individuals.
c. A team of organisational psychologists once set out to discover what makes some work groups more effective than others.

Where in paragraph 1 does the following sentence best fit?
'Delaying the task brings immediate, if temporary, relief from these emotions.'
questions.e: Câu chèn có 'these emotions' → phải đứng sau câu liệt kê cảm xúc (boredom, anxiety, self-doubt); câu ngay sau nó 'Unfortunately, this relief is short-lived' cần 'relief' ở câu trước → vị trí [III].
questions.ctx:
Almost everyone has, at some point, postponed an important task in favour of something more pleasant. [I] Procrastination is commonly regarded as a problem of poor time management, but psychologists increasingly see it in a different light. [II] In their view, people put off tasks not because they cannot plan their time, but because the tasks themselves trigger unpleasant feelings such as boredom, anxiety or self-doubt. [III] Unfortunately, this relief is short-lived, and the task usually becomes even more stressful as the deadline approaches. [IV]
This emotional explanation helps to account for a puzzling feature of procrastination: it is often most severe among people who care deeply about the outcome. A student who fears that an essay will not be good enough may find it easier to avoid starting altogether than to confront the possibility of failure. In this sense, procrastination can act as a kind of shield, protecting a person's self-image in the short term while damaging their performance in the long term.
If procrastination is rooted in emotion, then strategies that focus only on schedules and to-do lists are unlikely to be enough. Experts instead recommend approaches that make the first step less threatening. Breaking a large project into small, concrete actions, for example, reduces the sense of being overwhelmed. Some people also find it helpful to commit to working on a task for just five minutes; once they have started, continuing is often far easier than they expected.
Perhaps most importantly, researchers suggest treating oneself with understanding rather than harsh criticism after a lapse. Self-blame may seem like a way to stay motivated, but it tends to intensify the negative feelings that caused the delay in the first place.

questions.q: The word 'short-lived' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ______.
questions.e: 'short-lived' = tồn tại trong thời gian ngắn → 'brief'.

[II] In their view, people put off tasks not because they cannot plan their time, but because the tasks themselves trigger unpleasant feelings such as boredom, anxiety or self-doubt. [III] Unfortunately, this relief is short-lived, and the task usually becomes even more stressful as the deadline approaches. [IV]

questions.ctx:
Honeybees face a remarkable communication challenge. When a forager discovers a rich patch of flowers, she must somehow inform her sisters back at the hive where to find it, often in complete darkness. Her solution is a behaviour known as the waggle dance.
On the vertical surface of the honeycomb, the returning bee runs in a straight line while vibrating her body from side to side, then loops back to repeat the movement. The angle of this straight run relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food source relative to the sun. If the bee waggles straight upwards, for example, the flowers lie in the same direction as the sun; a run angled to the right signals that the food lies to the right of the sun by the same angle.
Distance is conveyed too. The longer the waggle portion of the dance lasts, the farther away the food is. Other bees follow the dancer closely, picking up both the movements and the scent of the flowers clinging to her body.
The dance was decoded in the mid-twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, whose work earned him a share of a Nobel Prize. His findings were initially met with scepticism, since few people believed that insects could communicate abstract information such as direction and distance. Later experiments, however, confirmed that bees really do use the information in the dance to locate food.
